body.text: In June 2027, Mongolia was supposed to have its first presidential election since the 2019 constitutional amendment, which limits the president to one six-year term. Even as the country was gearing up for the election, Mongolia’s sitting president, Khurelsukh Ukhnaa, abruptly resigned, pushing the country into a deep political crisis.

On November 17, Khurelsukh resigned abruptly, amid explosive corruption charges leveled against him from a political rival now based overseas. Mongolia’s parliament, which is controlled by Khurelsukh’s own Mongolian People’s Party (MPP), approved his resignation two days later, changing the political landscape for Mongolia’s 2027 presidential election, now set to be held in March.

The opposition Democratic Party was already eyeing the presidency, basing its campaign on charges that the MPP is politically corrupt. The MPP also faces questions of public confidence after a series of toppled governments: the ousting of Oyun-Erdene Luvsannamsrai in May 2025, followed by the resignation of Zandanshatar Gombojav in March 2026. To opposition parties and possible contenders, Khurelsukh’s resignation might have just widened that opportunity.

Khurelsukh was to be the first Mongolian president to serve a single six-year term after the 2019 constitutional amendment. The amendment was partially aimed at strengthening checks and balances among the three government bodies: the presidency, the State Great Khural (Mongolia’s parliament), and the Cabinet, led by the prime minister.

While the motivation for the change was domestic, giving the president a longer term also carried foreign policy implications by extending the time in office at the highest level of government. During his tenure, Khurelsukh has helped expand Ulaanbaatar’s global engagement, and diversify bilateral and multilateral relationships. Despite being encircled by China and Russia, both geographically and geopolitically, Mongolia was able to expand its “third neighbor” partners during Khurelsukh’s nearly six-year term.

In Northeast Asia, Mongolia sealed a strategic partnership with South Korea in 2021, upgraded bilateral relations with Japan to Special Strategic Partnership for Peace and Prosperity in 2022. These bilateral links brought deeper political, economic, and cultural links that will strengthen Ulaanbaatar’s landlocked position. The deepening of relations with Japan and South Korea is a clear indication of Northeast Asia’s changing geopolitics, and will allow Mongolia to seek trilateral opportunities with regional partners.

Mongolia also strengthened bilateral links with European (France, Germany, and Italy) and Turkic countries (Kazakhstan and Turkiye). While these relations all vary in substance, each of these bilateral links strengthens Ulaanbaatar’s foreign policy mechanisms at the highest level of government. This was especially important given the repeated instability in the Cabinet. The office of the president thus plays a pivotal role in expanding Mongolia’s footprint on the global stage.

Even with the upcoming election, however, Mongolia’s foreign policy direction will likely not be substantially changed. Mongolia’s strategic balancing act with Russia and China will continue to be pivotal, even as the country expands its cooperation with “third neighbors.” There are many moving parts in Northeast Asia that Ulaanbaatar can benefit from economically. These relationships and links have not previously been mingled with domestic politics, and that will remain true in 2027 and beyond.

Implementation of Mongolia’s foreign policy is only one element of the presidency, however. In addition to serving as chair of Mongolia’s National Security Council, and as commander-in-chief, the president has veto power over legislation.

Khurelsukh’s resignation raises question about institutional reform and governance. The infighting within the MPP illustrated the risks of having one-party-led governments. Opposition parties argue that the MPP’s internal shenanigans have now become a national security issue by causing major political instability. The DP will try to convince voters that the next election is an opportunity to end this cycle.

Institutional reform in Mongolia has been discussed before, including debates over whether to continue with parliamentary government or switch to a presidential system. Now that topic has been raised again amid continued political instability.

Perhaps to most important question ahead of the 2027 presidential election is whether political parties will field candidates free of corruption scandals and allegations. Mongolia’s score in the Corruption Perception Index has been on a downward slide since 2015, with the MPP in power for the majority of that time (since July 2016). Corruption allegations have fueled repeated protests, particularly since the “coal theft” protests of 2022.

Given the high-stake elections combined with the ongoing infighting within MPP, and the abrupt resignation of Khurelsukh, current speculation places a spotlight on DP candidates. The DP’s early primary contenders include former Prime Minister Altankhuyag Norov, former Chairman of the DP Gantomor Luvsannyam, and current MP Ganbat Dashdondog.

Although the political winds might seem to favor the DP, the Mongolian public seeks first and foremost a candidate free of corruption allegations, someone who can deliver institutional stability. And the MPP thinks it has found that candidate.

On November 22, the MPP chose ex-Prime Minister Zandanshatar Gombojav as a lead contender for the 2027 presidential race. At least within the MPP, the shared view is that Zamdanshatar is a key figure not hampered by major corruption allegations and scandals.

Khurelsukh’s resignation will force the election to move forward to March rather than being held in June 2027. This election will test whether Mongolia’s post-2019 constitutional framework can deliver institutional stability domestically. The election will not recalibrate Mongolia’s foreign policy and its global engagement but rather focus on domestic issues such as corruption, institutional reform, reducing government spending, and social welfare.

The next president, however, will still need to have the means to strengthen Ulaanbaatar’s global footprint, help implement many of Mongolia’s global pledges, and continue diversifying economic outlets in rapidly changing geopolitical landscape. What the country and the Mongolian people don’t need in these turbulent times is another leader playing politics.
